source.title: Customizing the Inductive Biases of Softmax Attention using Structured Matrices
source.authors: Yilun Kuang; Noah Amsel; Sanae Lotfi; Shikai Qiu; Andres Potapczynski; Andrew Gordon Wilson

record.file_problem: Whole paper, including appendices, is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps model width and training compute and reports held-out language-model validation loss against compute, but it does not fit or assess the power-law form itself.
record.gate_note: The OpenWebText results report comparative validation-loss curves against compute, which bear on loss scaling. The paper does not report fitted power-law exponents, extrapolation tests, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Results cited from other work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper proposing MLR and BTT attention scoring functions. The OpenWebText, Chronos and ETTh1 results compare the authors' attention variants against standard and sliding-window attention by plotting validation loss against compute. 'Scaling law' is used loosely to mean the loss-vs-compute curve. No power law is fitted, no exponent is reported, and nothing tests whether loss follows a power law. These are comparisons of the study's own method with alternatives, so T4 rather than a test of V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Add that the authors also conclude Bilinear BTT and Bilinear MLR scoring functions resolve the low-rank bottleneck on in-context regression, beating standard attention at fixed compute. Their 'improved scaling laws' claim means lower loss-vs-compute curves, not a fitted power law.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes the attention scoring structure and compares validation loss across model widths and compute; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting or allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: On OpenWebText, outcomes are compared across attention structures and model widths. In ETTh1, forecasting outcomes are evaluated at horizons 96, 192, and 336 hours; the text reports an association between horizon and relative MAE for the 4-level MLR configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: On character-level OpenWebText, 8-level MLR attention gives lower validation loss than standard, SWA and Global+SWA attention at matched non-embedding compute, across widths 256–768 (Fig. 4, 14).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLR attention attains lower validation loss per unit compute than standard and sliding-window attention in small character-level LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: MLR attention in Chronos gives slightly lower validation loss with fewer FLOPs. On ETTh1, its relative MAE improvement over standard attention is around 1% and grows with horizon.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: MLR attention can improve time-series validation loss or forecasting error relative to standard attention.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The relevant language-model results are presented as plots without numerical values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The paper describes improved scaling laws but gives no power-law fit, exponent, extrapolation evaluation, or compute-optimal allocation analysis.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Curves are used only to compare attention variants.
Attention-type changes are not depth or width shape changes at fixed parameter count. No test of shape insensitivity.
Time-series results compare attention variants. No power-law form is fitted.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V1 links is overturned. Loss-vs-compute curves serve only as a benchmark for the proposed attention method; the paper never assesses power-law form. All rows are own-method vs. comparator results.

versions.untested_parts: Tests validation loss against compute for one character-tokenized OpenWebText setup and several attention structures and widths. Does not fit or quantify a power law, report exponents, test loss against parameter count or tokens independently, or establish behavior over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for loss-minimizing parameter and token counts.
Does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture changes at fixed parameter count to test whether their effects are slight.
Time-series forecasting is evaluated, but no power-law form is fitted or tested in that regime.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, and no analysis of curves bending away from a fitted power law.
